quick: Take at the same time daily; consistent vitamin K intake
summary: Acenocoumarol is a short-acting coumarin (vitamin K antagonist) oral anticoagulant used to treat and prevent venous and arterial thromboembolism, including in atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and after prosthetic heart valves. It is not FDA-approved in the US (widely used in Europe, Latin America and Asia); this record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF. Dose is fully individualized to the INR (commonly target 2.0-3.0). It has many drug, food (vitamin K) and disease interactions, and bleeding is the principal risk; reversal is with vitamin K and, for major bleeds, prothrombin complex concentrate.
indications: Treatment and prevention of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism)
Prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in atrial fibrillation
Prevention of thromboembolism in other high-risk cardiac conditions

dosage.d: Typically 2-4 mg/day for the first 1-2 days (lower in elderly/at-risk), then adjust by INR
dosage.n: Avoid large loading doses; check INR early

dosage.d: ~1-8 mg/day titrated to the target INR (commonly 2.0-3.0)
dosage.n: Higher target (2.5-3.5) for some mechanical valves

dosage.c: Elderly / hepatic or renal impairment / high bleeding risk
dosage.d: Lower starting dose with cautious titration
Dose titrated to a higher INR target per valve type/position

admin: Take once daily at the same time each day (often evening) so INR results can guide same-day dose changes
Dose is set entirely by INR - never use a fixed dose without monitoring
Maintain a consistent dietary vitamin K intake (green leafy vegetables); avoid large swings
Avoid binge alcohol and review every new medicine for interactions
Carry an anticoagulant alert card and inform all clinicians/dentists before procedures
moa: Acenocoumarol inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K. This impairs gamma-carboxylation and hence the synthesis of functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S), producing a delayed anticoagulant effect once pre-formed factors are cleared.

absolute: Severe hepatic disease with coagulopathy / esophageal varices
Recent or planned surgery on the CNS or eye; conditions with high hemorrhage risk
relative: Poor adherence or inability to monitor INR

preg: Contraindicated, particularly in the first trimester - coumarins cross the placenta and cause embryopathy (nasal/skeletal abnormalities) and fetal bleeding/CNS abnormalities. Use heparin/LMWH instead during pregnancy where anticoagulation is required.
lact: Generally considered compatible with breastfeeding - only minimal amounts pass into milk and the infant's clotting is not usually affected; ensure the infant receives vitamin K per local practice.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; monitor INR more closely as anticoagulant response and bleeding risk may be increased.
hepatic: The anticoagulant effect is enhanced in hepatic impairment (reduced clotting-factor synthesis and altered drug metabolism); contraindicated in severe liver disease with coagulopathy and used cautiously with close INR monitoring otherwise.

major: Drugs increasing bleeding/INR: NSAIDs, aspirin, other anticoagulants/antiplatelets, azole antifungals (fluconazole, miconazole), metronidazole, cotrimoxazole, amiodarone, many antibiotics
Enzyme inducers decreasing effect (risk of clotting): rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, St John's wort
moderate: Statins, fibrates, thyroid hormones - can potentiate effect
minor: Many other drugs alter INR - review every new medication
interactions.food: Maintain consistent vitamin K intake; large amounts of green leafy vegetables or sudden dietary change can lower INR. Cranberry juice may increase INR.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid binge drinking; acute alcohol raises INR/bleeding risk and chronic heavy use can lower it - keep intake low and consistent.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs INR/prothrombin time (the basis of monitoring); affects coagulation assays.

serious: Skin necrosis (early, especially with protein C/S deficiency)
emergency: Signs of intracranial hemorrhage (severe headache, weakness, altered consciousness)

monitoring: INR regularly - frequently at initiation and after any dose/drug/diet change, then at stable intervals
Review of new medicines and dietary vitamin K consistency
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed at the same time daily and never change the dose without an INR result
Keep your diet (green vegetables) consistent and avoid sudden changes or binge drinking
Report unusual bleeding or bruising, black stools, red/brown urine, or a severe headache at once
Tell every doctor, dentist and pharmacist that you take an anticoagulant before any procedure or new medicine
Carry an anticoagulant alert card and keep all INR appointments
pk: Anticoagulant effect begins ~36-72 h (delay until clotting factors fall)
Plasma peak ~1-3 h; full INR effect after a few days
Anticoagulant effect lasts ~2 days after stopping
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the US but widely used elsewhere; this record uses EMA/SmPC and BNF references
Shorter half-life than warfarin - effect builds and reverses faster, allowing more responsive dose adjustment
Dose is ENTIRELY INR-guided (commonly target 2.0-3.0); never fixed-dose
Innumerable drug and vitamin-K (food) interactions - re-check INR after any change
Reverse with vitamin K (phytomenadione); use prothrombin complex concentrate (not just FFP) for major bleeding
missed: Take a missed dose on the same day if remembered; if not remembered until the next day, skip it and do NOT double up. Record the missed dose and tell the anticoagulation clinic, as it can affect the INR.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive anticoagulation and bleeding. Management depends on INR and bleeding: omit doses for minor over-anticoagulation; give oral/IV vitamin K (phytomenadione) for high INR; and for major bleeding give prothrombin complex concentrate (or fresh frozen plasma if unavailable) plus IV vitamin K, with supportive care.
